- When sentiment is strongly negative (avg < -0.3) over recent days, model tends to overcorrect downward → reduce forecast dip, avoid premature bottoming.  
- When sentiment is strongly positive (avg > 0.3) and price is rising, model often overshoots → cap forecast at 1–2% above recent peak or align with sentiment peak.  
- If model forecast shows sharp upward spike followed by steep decline, it often overreacts → dampen initial spike and smooth transition.  
- If true outcome shows mean reversion (price returns to prior 30-day average) after a spike, model often fails to recognize → adjust forecast to align with 30-day moving average if sentiment is neutral or mildly negative.  
- When sentiment history shows repeated short-term volatility (e.g., alternating +/– 0.3), model tends to overfit noise → use 5-day smoothing or ignore sentiment-driven outliers.  
- If model forecast is consistently 5–10% above true outcome over 30-day horizon, reduce forecast by 3–5% if sentiment is neutral or slightly positive.  
- If model forecast is consistently 5–10% below true outcome, increase forecast by 3–5% if sentiment is negative or market is recovering.  
- Avoid forecasting based solely on recent 18-day history if sentiment is diverging from historical patterns → use sentiment-weighted moving average or hybrid model.
